summary: The Gemara expounds each phrase of Numbers 19 regarding the red heifer, establishes that the Tsuk cliff is 12 mil from Jerusalem, details how the goat is pushed backward, and describes the signal relay system and the crimson thread that turned white as a sign of atonement.

display.whats: What does each phrase in the parah adumah verse teach, and what are the physical details of the Azazel goat ceremony?
display.hint: The Gemara is doing two things simultaneously: a verse-by-verse drasha of Numbers 19 (each word teaches a halakha about the parah rite) and filling in practical details of the Yom Kippur goat journey - the cliff distance, the manner of pushing, the signal system.
display.title: The Parah Verses, the Tsuk, and the Whitening Thread

learning.ahaMoment: The crimson thread turning white is Is. 1:18 fulfilled physically - 'though your sins be red as scarlet, they shall become white as snow.' The Temple era was when this verse was literally enacted.
learning.memoryAnchor: Crimson thread + backward push + 12-mil cliff: the ceremony was designed so there would be no ambiguity that the goat had truly been sent away and could not return.
learning.learnerQuestion: What halakhot does each phrase of the parah adumah verse yield, and what does it mean when the crimson thread fails to turn white?
learning.coreTension: The crimson thread's whitening is treated as a sign that atonement was accepted, but the thread did not always turn white even in Temple times, raising the question of whether the sending itself, not the sign, is what actually achieves atonement.
learning.coreMove: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's warning, 'do not rely on the thread - it is a sign but not the atonement itself,' resolves the tension: the verse-by-verse halakhot (12-mil Tsuk, backward push, signal relay, divided thread) establish a precisely defined ceremony whose efficacy does not depend on the thread turning white.

takeaway.text: The crimson thread turning white is a sign of atonement, not its cause; the goat's sending itself, carried out exactly as the verse-by-verse halakhot specify, is what achieves atonement, whether or not the thread whitens.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat the whitening thread as the mechanism of atonement itself, missing Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's point that it is only a sign and the goat's sending is what actually atones.

rashiTranslations.en: Who brought out a donkey along with it - for according to the first Tanna it is permitted, since there is no concern that people will say to Rabbi
that it is forbidden, since it is the word 'it' that is written. 'And Elazar the priest shall take' - regarding the receiving of its blood.
To Shmuel - who deduces from 'before him' that a non-priest is valid for the slaughtering, it was necessary to write
'Elazar' regarding the receiving of the blood, to return it to Elazar; for if it had written 'and he shall take of its blood'
(and sprinkle with his finger) it would imply that it refers back to the one who slaughters,
the same person as the slaughterer. To Rav, who also says the slaughtering
is performed by Elazar, there was no need to write
'Elazar' regarding the receiving; and since it is written, it is a restriction
following a restriction - 'to Elazar' and not another - and there is no
restriction following a restriction, etc. 'And the priest shall take
cedar wood' - to Shmuel, who says the receiving and sprinkling
were performed by Elazar, here 'priest' is written to make valid
the casting of the cedar wood by an ordinary priest; this
is an implication that excludes directly from another implication, and likewise
all these that we say follow this pattern. And to Rav, who validates the receiving
by an ordinary priest, this implication stands on its own
and does not exclude from the verse before it,
and it was necessary to write 'priest' in it; for if it had written
'and he shall take cedar wood' without writing 'priest,' we would
have said that anyone who wishes may take it, and we would not
establish it upon the priest of the receiving; one might
have thought, since it is not itself the body of the heifer ritual, that a priest is not needed, etc.
'The priest in his priesthood' - this 'priest' is a superfluous word,
for it need not have been written except
'and he shall wash his garments,' etc., and I would know
that it refers to the one who was just being discussed; rather, it comes to juxtapose
'priest' with 'his garments,' meaning that it is performed in the garments of priesthood
and not in ordinary garments. 'And the priest shall be impure
until evening' - to teach about the heifer that is performed
for future generations, that it too requires the garments of priesthood. 'This works out well
according to the one who says' - above, that for future generations it is performed by an ordinary
priest and does not derive the statute from the Day
of Atonement; it was necessary to write 'priest' here
to teach about the one performed for future generations, that it be done in the garments
of priesthood.' 'A man - to validate the non-priest' - because
just before it the discussion concerns a priest, here it is written
'a man,' to validate the non-priest; for if it had written 'and he shall gather
the ash of the heifer,' we would have said 'priest,'
since just before it the discussion concerns a priest; it writes here
'a man.' 'To validate the woman' - for if
it were only to exclude an impure person, that is obvious, since the Torah calls it
a sin-offering. 'To sanctify' - to place water upon
the ash in an earthenware vessel. 'And they shall take, for the impure person' -
after 'and a pure man shall gather' it is written; this is
the service that comes after the gathering, and it writes 'and they shall take,'
referring to those mentioned in the gathering - a non-priest
and a woman, but not a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor. 'If so' -
since it refers back to what precedes, let it say 'and he shall take,' since
regarding the gathering it was written in the singular. 'A woman -
from where does he derive it?' And likewise an androgyne, because of
the uncertainty of being a woman. 'And the Rabbis' say to you: actually
it refers back to what precedes, and the reason it was not written 'and he shall take'
in the singular is that if it had written 'and he shall take and give,' we would have said that only when one person takes the ash
and he himself gives it upon the water; it therefore writes 'and they shall take,' to teach that even if two take it, it is valid. 'And he shall take
hyssop' - for this is written regarding the sprinkling of its water, and it is the service that comes after the sanctification. To the Rabbis -
who say the sanctification is performed with the water of that same gathering, and regarding the gathering 'a man'
pure is written, meaning a non-priest and a woman are valid, you must say that 'a man, pure' here does not come to validate
a non-priest and a woman, nor to disqualify a minor, and to be an implication standing on its own; for if so, the verse should have been silent
about it and simply written 'and he shall take hyssop and dip it in water and sprinkle,' and I would know that it refers to that same
matter mentioned before it; and since it does write it, to teach 'a man and not a woman,' you must say
that this implication excludes directly from another implication. 'Pure - to validate a minor' - since he disqualified him
regarding the sanctification. And according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says a woman is invalid for the sanctification and a minor
is valid, this comes to teach the opposite: 'a man' but not a minor, 'pure' to validate
a woman; for one cannot say it is an implication standing on its own, since if so the verse should have been silent about it.
